name: ep-curve
renderNote: The curves, their points, the return-period and loss axes and the curve names are one `<svg>`. The return period runs across on a log scale, so 1-in-10, 1-in-100 and 1-in-1,000 are evenly spaced, and the loss climbs a linear axis from zero.

projection.frame: each point is the loss to expect once in that many years, the return period across on a log scale

description: An exceedance-probability curve: the loss to expect once every N years, with return periods across on a log scale and up to four curves (OEP and AEP, gross and net).
purpose: Use when the question is how big a loss to plan for: a reinsurance program's 1-in-100 and 1-in-250 losses, a cat model's output, a capital model's tail. Each point is `{return period, loss}`; a curve is a name with its points nested under it.

title.description: Slide heading — name the loss the audience should remember ('A 1-in-100 year costs $410M'), not 'EP curve'.

axes.description: Optional axis line, as ONE bracketed list in its own paragraph ABOVE the heading: the return-period axis, then the loss axis — `[{Return period, 10..250}, {Loss}]`. A return-period domain of at least 1 widens the axis past the points (a minimum below 1 is ignored); a loss domain raises the ceiling, while the floor stays zero or the lowest loss. The return-period axis is always log, so `log` changes nothing. Without the line the x axis is captioned 'Return period'. Same idiom as `scatter` and `histogram`.

curves.description: A flat list of point records draws one curve: `` `{100, $410M}` `` is a 1-in-100 year loss of $410M, return period first. For several curves, write each curve's name and nest its points under it: `- OEP` then `  - `{100, $410M}``. Up to four curves; a return period below 1 is not a point.

stressDoc.summary: Four curves, eight return periods from 1-in-2 to 1-in-1,000.

whenToUse.title: How big a loss to plan for
whenToUse.body: An EP curve earns its slide when the question is the size of a rare loss: the 1-in-100 a program must cover, how much a reinsurance tower takes off the gross curve. For how often each loss band happens, use `histogram`.

whenToUse.title: Two to four curves
whenToUse.body: OEP and AEP, or gross and net, read best together: the gap between the curves is the story. Past four, split the slide.

antiPatterns.title: Return period written as a label
antiPatterns.body: `- 1-in-100 `$410M`` is a label and a value, which the chart cannot place. Write the point record, return period first: `` `{100, $410M}` ``; the axis prints `1-in-100` for you.

antiPatterns.title: A probability instead of a return period
antiPatterns.body: Write the return period, not the annual probability: 1% is `{100, …}`, 0.4% is `{250, …}`.

related.name: histogram
related.when: how often each band of loss happens, rather than the loss at each return period

related.name: tower
related.when: the reinsurance program the curve is priced against

related.name: line
related.when: a quantity over time, on an evenly spaced axis

commonMistakes.fix: The record is `{return period, loss}`: the return period runs across the bottom, the way the chart is drawn.

dataShapeGuidance: Each point is `{return period, loss}`: the return period a number of years of at least 1, the loss any number Segno reads (`$410M`, `410`).
A curve's points are drawn in return-period order whatever the order written; a return period given twice in one curve keeps the first.
`lint:deck` names a point it cannot read (a thousands separator, `{1,000, $900M}`, is the commonest), a return period given twice in one curve, and a fifth curve.

budget.note: Counted in CURVES. Editorial: each curve's name sits at its right end, so a narrow pane holds two before the names crowd.

pane.review: side 25 and stack 30 measured with tools/measure-pane-fit.js: the first two curves fit at every size it tries (25 to 65 side, 30 to 60 stack).

venueCapacity.none: A chart scales its marks to the box instead of clipping, so no count marks where it stops fitting.
